name: Figures — 350,000 patent drawings as an infinite wall
one_liner: A free, no-signup wall of 350,000 US design-patent drawings you can scroll, search in plain English ("folding chair", "camera grip", "toaster"), and pull one out to see every figure of that invention plus a one-line plain-English description and a link to the patent.
problem: For industrial designers, engineers, 3D-print hobbyists, illustrators and the "look at this weird old invention" crowd: patent drawings are some of the most beautiful public-domain line art ever made, and there is no good way to just look at them. Google Patents and Espacenet are text-first legal search tools — you type a classification code and get a results list of documents, with the drawing buried inside a PDF. Nobody has built the Pinterest view. Figures makes the drawing the result: an infinite dense grid of line art you can scroll like a mood board, filter by decade and Locarno/USPC design class, and search semantically rather than by patent jargon.
target_customer: Designers, makers and engineers on X, r/Design, r/industrialdesign, r/3Dprinting, Hacker News and the design-Twitter crowd that shares roomGPT-style one-input toys; also patent attorneys and IP paralegals who would use it as a fast prior-art eyeball pass.
why_now: The DeepPatent dataset (Los Alamos / GoFigure-LANL) puts 350,000+ segmented design-patent drawings in clean PNG under CC0, with patent IDs attached, and DeepPatent2 extends it past 2 million drawings under CC BY 4.0 — no scraping, no USPTO API key, no rate limit. Cheap CLIP-class image embeddings plus a browser-side vector index now make semantic search over a few hundred thousand thumbnails feasible on a static site, which was not realistic to ship in a weekend a year or two ago.
comparables: Google Patents and Espacenet (120M+ and 150M+ documents) — exhaustive and free, but text-first: the drawing is an artifact inside a PDF, never the browsing unit. PNNL's Visual Intellectual Property Search (vips.pnnl.gov) — genuinely visual patent discovery, but scoped to DOE-lab IP, not the whole design-patent corpus. Thingiverse — the right browsing pattern (dense grid, categories) for a different corpus of user-uploaded 3D models. DeepPatent/DeepPatent2 exist as research datasets with retrieval benchmarks but no public browsable front end. Figures differs by being drawing-first, semantic-search-first, and free with no account — the shelf-of-books presentation this builder's taste file already admires, applied to a corpus nobody has presented well.
risks: It can be a one-time toy: people scroll for five minutes, post one screenshot and never return — the fix is giving designers a reason to come back (saved boards, a weekly "figures of the week" grid, a download-as-reference button). Google Patents already has all of this data, so the entire value is presentation; if the grid is slow or the search returns mush, there is nothing left. Client-side semantic search over 50k+ vectors has real browser-memory and first-load limits, which is the one dependency that could force a fallback to keyword-plus-class filtering.
build_plan: Stack: Next.js static export on Vercel, no backend. (1) Download DeepPatent (CC0, Google Drive, 9 parts), keep a 50k–100k subset of the cleanest drawings and their patent IDs; (2) batch-embed thumbnails with an open CLIP-class image encoder locally, embed nothing at request time; (3) precompute a text-queryable index: embed a few thousand candidate query phrases, or ship a quantized text encoder in the browser via transformers.js so the search box runs client-side with no API cost; (4) generate 256px webp thumbnails to a CDN plus a JSON shard per class/decade; (5) front end: infinite virtualised grid, search box, decade and design-class filters, and a detail view with all figures for that patent, the title, the year, the assignee and a deep link to Google Patents; (6) a 'copy as reference image' and 'share this grid' link that encodes the query in the URL so a search result is postable. Cut: full 350k on day one (ship 50k), per-image AI captions, sketch-to-search upload, user accounts, anything needing a server.
launch_post:
I turned 350,000 public-domain US patent drawings into one infinite scrollable wall.

Type "folding chair" or "camera grip" and watch a century of line art appear. Click any figure for every sheet of that patent.

Free, no signup, open source. CC0 data from the DeepPatent dataset.
reasoning: Won the build track because every dependency checks out: the dataset is confirmed CC0, confirmed downloadable, confirmed ~350k images with patent IDs, and the search can run entirely client-side so there is no per-query cost and no rate limit to blow up on launch day. It matches the taste file almost exactly — the 'research papers as a shelf of books' pattern applied to a corpus that is inherently more beautiful — and it is one screenshot that explains itself. It beat the agent-tooling build candidates because those all crowd the same developer audience as past library entries (Shelf, Skillscope) and because the agent-readiness and MCP-risk scanner space already has multiple free tools. Pain is latent — nobody is asking for a patent-drawing browser — so the thing that makes people notice it is the first screenshot of the wall itself, which is why the launch post is mostly the demo.
candidates_considered:
VENTURE
1. Mandate — approval gate + E&O evidence record for AI client communications in independent insurance agencies. KEPT: verified a real adoption/governance gap (46% AI use vs 13% with a policy), a named buyer with a budget line, and competitors that each miss the cross-tool pre-send gate.
2. Portal Clerk — deterministic portal-submission robot with human approval and audit for freight brokers / permit filers, inspired by Pomerado. DROPPED: the same buyer and workflow are already contested by Vooma (~$16.6M raised), HappyRobot (~$200M raised, Series C Aug 2026), Drumkit ($1,500/mo pilots) and Skyvern ($29–$149/mo self-serve), and the freight wedge in particular is well funded; no narrow buyer left that a small team reaches first.
3. Agent Attribution Desk — a "who did what" ledger across a person's many personal agents, from @sriramk's post. DROPPED on feasibility, not desire: the Gmail and Calendar user APIs do not expose which OAuth client made a change (actor-app attribution is a Workspace admin audit-log feature), so the core promise cannot be delivered for the consumer/prosumer buyer the post describes.
4. Clinic send-gate (dental/medical front-office version of Mandate). DROPPED as the weaker twin: HIPAA, BAAs and EHR integration make the first version months longer, and Weave/Arini/Assort already own the channel; same idea, harder entry.

BUILD
1. Figures — 350,000 CC0 design-patent drawings as a searchable infinite wall. KEPT: dataset confirmed CC0 and downloadable, search runs client-side so there is no API cost, and no free drawing-first browser exists (Google Patents and Espacenet are text-first; PNNL VIPS is DOE-only).
2. Agent X-ray for any website — paste a URL, see what an AI agent could actually do there. DROPPED: at least five free scanners already do this (AI Agent Readiness Scanner, Frase, Web Specification, agentready, Cloudflare's isitagentready), plus a crowd of free agentic-commerce readiness scanners.
3. MCP capability card — one-screen plain-English list of every action an MCP server exposes, with destructive ones flagged. DROPPED: close prior art in MCP Permission Scanner and mcp-risk, and it serves the same developer audience as the library's existing Shelf and Skillscope.
4. Interface Grammar — turn a screenshot or OpenAPI spec into the nouns and verbs an agent should operate on, from @Mappletons' post. DROPPED: genuinely little prior art, but the output is an abstract diagram rather than something anyone would post, and the input (a design file) is too fiddly for a one-box toy.
5. Genie 4 world-model toy. DROPPED on access: Genie 4 is trusted-tester only, with no public API, no pricing and no general availability — nothing to build on this weekend.
research_notes:
22 tool calls budgeted; 20 used (3 reading, 10 venture, 7 build). I cannot see images, so for the four video-only bookmarks I relied on post text plus Web Summary.

Reading (3): Summarised DigitalOcean's Action Gateway — confirmed the allow/deny/ask-a-human policy model and that it is sold to developer teams, which became the venture's "why now" and its explicit contrast (the same pattern, repackaged for a non-technical regulated SMB). Summarised Pomerado (YC F26) — confirmed it generates deterministic integrations from a described website workflow, which spawned the Portal Clerk candidate. Summarised Genie 4 — the finding that it is trusted-tester only with no public API or pricing killed the world-model build candidate before it cost me any build-pot calls.

Venture (10): Two keyword searches on agent attribution and approval tooling returned mostly SEO filler and were close to wasted. The productive calls were Perplexity summaries that each reshaped the candidate: a scan of agent-governance platforms showed everything is enterprise-priced (Microsoft Agent 365 $15/user/mo, IBM from $3,500/mo) or platform-locked, which pushed me away from a generic governance play; a property-management/insurance approval-workflow summary surfaced OfficeAgent at $149–$399/mo, proving the approve-before-send pattern sells at SMB prices; the Big "I" summary produced the decisive numbers (46% AI use in 2026 vs 15% in 2024, 8% with AI in daily workflow, 13% with a formal AI policy, 24%/22% naming compliance and inaccurate outputs) and named Covera, Trussed, Smarsh, Magellan and FieldWatch; a follow-up on Covera and Trussed established that Covera is a doer with its own review trail rather than a neutral cross-tool gate — that distinction is now the whole wedge. A Gmail/Calendar API check killed the agent-attribution venture on feasibility. Freight and Skyvern summaries (Vooma ~$16.6M, HappyRobot ~$200M and a reported ~$250k minimum, Drumkit $1,500/mo pilot, Skyvern $29–$149/mo with human-in-the-loop gated to Enterprise) closed the portal-automation gap for a solo builder.

Build (7): Checked prior art for the agent-readiness scanner (five free tools found — dropped), the MCP capability card (MCP Permission Scanner and mcp-risk found — dropped), and interface-grammar extraction (little prior art, but weak as a shareable toy). Then three calls on patent imagery: confirmed Google Patents BigQuery does not include drawing images and USPTO ODP has no per-drawing image endpoint (20 downloads per file per key per year), compared paid routes (SerpApi, EPO OPS 4GB/week free, PatentsView keys suspended), and finally confirmed DeepPatent — 350,000+ PNG design-patent drawings with patent IDs, CC0, direct download, plus DeepPatent2 at 2M+ under CC BY 4.0. That last finding is what moved Figures from "needs a paid API, probably too expensive" to buildable in a weekend with zero per-query cost, and is why buildability scored 7 rather than 4. A search for an existing patent-drawing gallery found only research papers (DeepPatent retrieval benchmarks), a DOE-scoped visual search at PNNL, and museum exhibits — no free consumer-facing wall.
prototype_summary: Figures is a searchable infinite wall of inline-SVG patent drawings where typing a word or two instantly reflows the grid into matching figures, with a shuffle button, decade/class filters, and a slide-over detail panel showing all figures for a patent.
